analysis.one_liner: Bars bailout recipients from paying executives bonuses promised under older contracts.
analysis.headline: A bill to close the bailout-bonus loophole drew 40 House cosponsors but never received a hearing or vote and died in committee.
analysis.plain_summary: In early 2009, Congress had banned companies bailed out with taxpayer money from paying executive bonuses, but wrote in an exception: bonuses required by contracts signed before February 11, 2009 were still payable. This bill would delete that exception, retroactively treating the ban as if it had always covered those older contract bonuses. It applied to firms that received help under the 2008 financial bailout program. It never got a committee hearing or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers who funded the bailout would keep more of their money, since bailed-out firms could no longer point to pre-existing contracts to justify bonus payments to executives.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the exception that let companies receiving federal bailout assistance pay bonuses required by written employment contracts signed on or before February 11, 2009 [S2].
Does this by striking clause (iii) from the compensation rules added by the 2009 economic recovery act, and applies the compensation limits as if that exception had never existed [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Executives at bailed-out financial firms, who would lose legally promised bonus payments, and the firms that would face the cost and possible legal claims for breaking those contracts.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have applied to bonus contracts already signed, meaning the government would be rewriting binding private contracts after the fact, which raises legal questions and could invite lawsuits from executives and the firms employing them [S3].

By the time it was introduced, many of the disputed bonuses had reportedly already been paid out, so the bill would do little to recover money that had left the firms; it mainly prevents future reliance on the exception [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to taxpayers is real but narrow: it affects bonuses at the handful of firms that took federal bailout money, not executive pay across the economy. The main cost is legal uncertainty around retroactively overriding signed contracts, plus the possibility of litigation with firms the government already had a financial stake in. Given that taxpayer money was involved and public anger over bailout bonuses was intense, the tradeoff most supporters would accept, but it is a targeted fix, not a broad solution.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 18, 2009, by Rep. Steven LaTourette with an initial group of Republican cosponsors, and was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services that same day [S1][S3].
A total of 40 House Republicans cosponsored the bill [S4].
The full action history shows only two actions: introduction and referral to committee. No hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled [S5].
The bill addressed the exception written into the 2009 economic recovery act that allowed TARP recipients to keep paying bonuses under contracts signed before February 11, 2009 [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Executives at bailout recipients kept the contract-based bonus exception, and the House Republican cosponsors avoided a recorded vote on the issue.

for.name: Rep. Steven C. LaTourette
for.role: Sponsor, House Financial Services Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the pre-existing-contract bonus exception for TARP recipients.

for.name: 40 of 178 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it formal backing from more than a fifth of the House Republican caucus.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 40 cosponsors were Republicans, and the Democratic-controlled Financial Services Committee never acted on it; no recorded votes exist to show broader support or opposition.

industries.industry: Bailed-out banks and financial firms (TARP recipients)
industries.note: The bill would have stripped the exception letting them pay bonuses required by contracts signed before February 11, 2009, at firms propped up with taxpayer funds. Their interest in keeping the exception ran against taxpayers who funded the bailout [S2].
Executives with pre-existing bonus contracts at bailout recipients would have lost legally promised payments. Because the bill died, those payments were preserved [S3].
